title: Postmortem: Dedicated capacity starvation on gpu-pool-delta
author: Connor O'Brien
content:
## Summary
On 2026-03-10, Dedicated customers on gpu-pool-delta saw rising queueing delays and request timeouts caused by capacity starvation. Total GPU count in the pool was adequate, but GPU fragmentation combined with misconfigured priority weights kept some large-model replicas from being scheduled in time.

## Customer impact
- Duration: 1 hour 12 minutes
- Symptoms: growing queue depth; p95 latency +40%; intermittent 504s
- Scope: Dedicated customers mapped to gpu-pool-delta in us-east-1

## Detection
- Alert: dedicated queue depth > threshold
- Customer Success escalation reporting timeouts on a pinned dedicated endpoint

## Timeline (UTC)
- 17:42: Queue depth alerts fire
- 17:55: Infra on-call finds fragmentation plus a weight misconfiguration
- 18:10: Mitigation: two tenants moved to gpu-pool-charlie; scheduler restarted with corrected weights
- 18:54: Queue depth back to normal

## Root cause
A change to the dedicated scheduler's priority weights did not account for GPU packing constraints of large models. Placement began favoring small replicas, which fragmented free GPUs and starved the large replicas that need contiguous resources.

## Contributing factors
- Scheduler weight changes are not run through a packing simulation in CI
- Capacity dashboards have no fragmentation metrics

## Follow-up action items
1. Add fragmentation metrics ("largest contiguous block", "packing efficiency") to capacity dashboards. Owner team: Infrastructure. Priority: P1.
2. CI simulation for scheduler weight changes with representative tenant/model mixes. Owner team: Infrastructure. Priority: P1.
3. SLO alert on dedicated queueing time (in addition to depth), wired to paging. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P0.
4. Dedicated pool rebalancing runbook with safe tenant moves and a comms template. Owner team: Customer Success. Priority: P2.

## Lessons learned
Dedicated reliability hinges on scheduler correctness and on being able to see fragmentation. We need simulations and better metrics to catch quiet capacity starvation before customers do.
